clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in ECM1 (extracellular matrix protein 1), leading to deposition of hyaline material in skin, mucosae and viscera
A hoarse cry or weak, husky voice from early infancy, due to infiltration of the vocal cords, is often the earliest and most characteristic feature
Moniliform blepharosis, a row of beaded waxy papules along the eyelid margins, is a classic diagnostic clue
Skin lesions evolve from early blistering and pox-like scars to waxy yellow papules, plaques and verrucous, hyperkeratotic lesions over extensor and friction sites
Infiltration of the tongue produces a firm, woody organ with restricted protrusion, and the frenulum may become thickened and bound down
Bilateral bean- or sickle-shaped calcification in the medial temporal lobes (amygdala) is frequently seen on imaging and is associated with epilepsy and impaired recognition of fear
Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture with PAS-positive hyaline deposits on biopsy, confirmed by ECM1 sequencing; management is supportive as no specific therapy exists
reference.pathophysiology: Lipoid proteinosis is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ECM1, which encodes extracellular matrix protein 1, a glycoprotein important in basement membrane structure, dermal homeostasis and regulation of growth factors and collagen organisation. ECM1 deficiency disrupts the dermo-epidermal junction and perivascular connective tissue, leading to progressive deposition of amorphous, periodic acid-Schiff-positive hyaline material composed of excess basement membrane components and disordered collagen around blood vessels, adnexa and at the epidermal-dermal interface. This infiltration thickens and stiffens the skin and mucosae, while similar deposition and dystrophic calcification within the brain, particularly the amygdala, account for the neurological and neuropsychiatric features.
additionalDifferentials: Erythropoietic protoporphyria and other cutaneous porphyrias with photosensitivity and scarring
Systemic sclerosis or other causes of a bound-down tongue and skin
additionalInvestigations: Skin or mucosal biopsy showing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant hyaline deposits around vessels and at the dermo-epidermal junction
ECM1 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Brain CT or MRI to detect characteristic medial temporal lobe calcification
Laryngoscopy to assess vocal cord and upper airway infiltration
Neuropsychological and psychiatric assessment where cognitive or behavioural features are present
redFlags: Progressive airway compromise from laryngeal and pharyngeal infiltration
Seizures related to temporal lobe involvement
Feeding or swallowing difficulty from tongue and oropharyngeal deposition
Corneal or ocular involvement threatening vision
reference.prognosis: Lipoid proteinosis generally follows a benign, slowly progressive course with a normal life expectancy, though hoarseness, cutaneous scarring and neurological features such as epilepsy may persist lifelong. Airway compromise is uncommon but can require intervention, and the overall outlook is determined largely by the extent of laryngeal and neurological involvement.
pitfalls: Attributing lifelong hoarseness to recurrent laryngitis rather than recognising it as an early sign of the disease
Confusing the hyaline deposits with amyloid, which requires Congo red staining and clinicopathological correlation to distinguish
Overlooking the diagnosis in a child with unexplained scarring, beaded eyelid papules and a husky voice
Failing to image the brain and missing epilepsy-associated temporal lobe calcification
Not offering genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition
management: No curative therapy exists; management is symptomatic, with oral dimethyl sulfoxide and oral retinoids such as acitretin tried for skin and mucosal deposits with variable benefit
Provide voice and airway care with laryngoscopic surveillance, and surgical removal of vocal-cord deposits by CO2 laser or microlaryngoscopy where hoarseness is severe or the airway is compromised
Treat cosmetically or functionally significant skin lesions with dermabrasion or laser
Control epilepsy related to medial temporal-lobe (amygdala) calcification with antiseizure medication
Offer neuropsychological and psychiatric support for cognitive and behavioural features
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across dermatology, ENT, neurology and clinical genetics
Provide genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance of the ECM1 defect
